entries.clue: Cancelled tax as not working (3-4)

blocks.note: a fixture that has been cancelled is off
duty is the tax charged on goods brought into a country

annotation.surface: A tax dropped because nothing is running.
annotation.walkthrough: Duty here is the customs charge, not the sense of obligation the surface leans on. 'Off' for cancelled is the everyday British use: a match is off when it will not be played.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone off duty is not working — their shift has ended and the job's demands are suspended until it starts again.

entries.clue: Fancy gold design finish on tea set (6)

indicatorNotes.finish: The finish of a word is the letter it stops at, so only that final letter of the word before it is taken.
indicatorNotes.set: Something set has been laid out the way somebody wanted it, and letters laid out afresh do not keep the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: or is gold in heraldry, the tincture of the metal
the letter this word finishes on
the three letters of the drink, laid out in a new order

annotation.surface: A gilded pattern painted round the rim of a tea service.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' is the adjective, not the verb, which is what lets it open the clue without looking like a definition. A tea set is a real object in the surface and three loose letters in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Ornate means heavily decorated — carved, gilded, curlicued — which is the showy sense of 'fancy' applied to an object.

entries.clue: Father’s opponents crossing imaginary land in Disney film (6)

indicatorNotes.crossing: What crosses something lies over it and out the other side, so the letters just named open up and the next chunk sits in the gap.

blocks.note: Fr is how a Catholic priest's title is written in front of his name
bridge players are named for the compass points, and East and North sit on opposite sides of the table
Oz is the country over the rainbow in The Wizard of Oz

annotation.surface: A priest's enemies straying across some make-believe country.
annotation.walkthrough: Bridge supplies the opponents: the game seats four players at the compass points, and any two next to each other are on opposing sides. 'Father' wants to be somebody's dad and is a priest.
annotation.definitionFit: Frozen is Disney's animation of the two royal sisters, one of whom turns her kingdom to ice.

entries.clue: Not planned to be nude, except accidentally (10)

indicatorNotes.accidentally: What happens accidentally happens in no arranged order, so these letters come out in an order nobody chose.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, the comma between them counting for nothing

annotation.surface: Somebody caught with no clothes on entirely by mistake.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Accidentally' sits where a solver expects an adverb describing the nudity, and is really the instruction. Ten letters of fodder for a ten-letter answer means nothing else is hiding in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Something unexpected is something nobody saw coming, which is what has not been planned for.

entries.clue: Year working with Kardashians on vacation: a long time (5)

indicatorNotes.on vacation: A word on vacation has been emptied out, with only the letters standing at its two ends left behind.

blocks.note: y is the standard short form of year
a machine that is working is on
the first and last letters of the name, all that survives the emptying

annotation.surface: A year spent holidaying with the famous reality-television family.
annotation.walkthrough: The Kardashians are the American reality-TV dynasty, wheeled in for their outside letters alone. 'On vacation' is the American word for a holiday and the crossword's instruction to gut a word at the same time.
annotation.definitionFit: Yonks is British slang for ages — 'I haven't seen her in yonks' — so it names a long stretch of time.

entries.clue: Often superheroes’ resolution is much appreciated thing (7)

blocks.note: comic-book heroes are often gods, Thor and Wonder Woman among them, and 'often' admits it is not always so
a story's resolution is where it ends

annotation.surface: The way superhero stories tend to wrap up is welcome news.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Resolution' offers the New Year kind and the plot kind, and only the plot kind hands over letters. The possessive apostrophe belongs to the surface and nothing else.
annotation.definitionFit: A godsend is a piece of luck arriving exactly when it is needed, welcome enough to feel sent from above.

entries.clue: Channel for wine-makers’ gossip? (9)

blocks.note: on the surface a watercourse or a television station belonging to people who make wine; in the answer, the plant their whole trade grows on
news that travels from person to person without ever being published, and the route it takes is the thing being named

annotation.surface: A television channel made by and for wine producers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I heard it on the grapevine' is the phrase the clue leans on, and the question mark admits that a climbing plant is not really a channel. Wine-makers own the vine; everybody else owns the saying.
annotation.definitionFit: A grapevine is the plant a wine-maker grows, and 'the grapevine' is the unofficial route along which gossip reaches you.

entries.clue: Money owing, busted suspect leaves America (4)

indicatorNotes.suspect: What is suspect cannot be trusted to be what it appears, so these letters are not to be trusted in the order they are handed over.
indicatorNotes.leaves: To leave is to walk out, so the letters named after it go, and only what stays behind is used.

blocks.note: six letters to start from
US is the States, and it is the pair that walks out, leaving four letters

annotation.surface: A caught suspect skipping the country while still owing money.
annotation.walkthrough: The suspect does not leave America; America leaves 'busted'. Four letters survive the departure, and they will not stay in the order they were left in.
annotation.definitionFit: A debt is money owed to somebody else and not yet paid back.

entries.clue: Characters among select rich charged (8)

indicatorNotes.Characters among: The characters among some words are the letters standing inside them, read in the order they already sit in.

blocks.note: eight consecutive letters, starting inside the first word and ending inside the second

annotation.surface: A few individuals among the wealthy elite facing charges.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charged' reads as facing a court and means carrying a current. Hidden words rearrange nothing, so the only move is finding where the run begins.
annotation.definitionFit: An electric fence, or an electric atmosphere, is one carrying a charge — literal in the first case, felt in the second.

entries.clue: Offended, opening document with poor wording (3,5)

indicatorNotes.opening: The opening of a word is the letter it begins with, so only that first letter of what follows is taken.
indicatorNotes.poor: Wording that is poor has not come out as it should, so these letters are not left in the order they were given.

blocks.note: the first letter of the word, which is what its opening is
seven letters of fodder, which the single letter above brings up to eight

annotation.surface: Somebody taking offence at a badly drafted document as they open it.
annotation.walkthrough: Seven letters of 'wording' cannot fill eight squares, and the document's own opening letter is the eighth. The comma after 'Offended' is the only mark separating definition from wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To offend, in its older moral sense, is to do wrong: to commit the offence rather than to hurt somebody's feelings.

entries.clue: Bouquet includes love knot (5)

indicatorNotes.includes: What a thing includes is held within it, so the letter named next sits inside the ones before it.

blocks.note: the nose of a wine is its bouquet, the smell that comes off the glass
love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as a zero

annotation.surface: A bunch of flowers with a love-knot tied into it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bouquet' is the wine-taster's word for a smell, not the flowers the surface hands you. A love knot really is a knot, which is how the definition slips by unnoticed.
annotation.definitionFit: A noose is the running knot at the end of a hangman's rope, the kind that tightens as it is pulled.

entries.clue: Red banana served as Indian side (4,5)

indicatorNotes.served: Something served up has been dished out in whatever arrangement the kitchen chose, so the letters need not keep the order they came in.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, filling both words of the answer

annotation.surface: A ripe red banana brought out alongside a curry.
annotation.walkthrough: Naan is the flatbread baked against the wall of a tandoor oven. 'Naan bread' therefore says bread twice over, which purists dislike and the grid requires.
annotation.definitionFit: A naan bread is the flatbread ordered alongside a curry, the standard side dish of an Indian restaurant menu.

entries.clue: In Paris, very old-fashioned Republican’s unwelcome visitor (10)

blocks.note: très is French for very, and 'in Paris' is what asks for the French
passé, another French import, means out of date
R is the letter beside a Republican's name on an American ballot, against D for a Democrat

annotation.surface: A thoroughly dated Republican turning up in Paris where nobody wants him.
annotation.walkthrough: Two French words in a row: the first is flagged by 'in Paris', the second so naturalised in English that no flag is needed. Both drop their accents, as crosswords always do.
annotation.definitionFit: A trespasser is somebody on land they have no right to be on, which makes them a visitor nobody invited.

entries.clue: Disturbance in prison (4)

blocks.note: the commotion a piece of news causes when it gets out
old criminal slang for jail, heard in the phrase for a man doing time inside

annotation.surface: Trouble breaking out behind bars.
annotation.walkthrough: Two nouns and no wordplay at all, with 'in' doing nothing but joining them. The jail sense is the one worth banking: four letters, and it turns up whenever a clue mentions prison.
annotation.definitionFit: A stir is a commotion or fuss, the sort a scandal causes; stir is also old slang for prison, as in serving a stretch in stir.

entries.clue: Sit down in shock inspiring prayer and article by church (4,1,5)

indicatorNotes.inspiring: To inspire is literally to breathe in, so what follows is drawn inside the letters already named.

blocks.note: a shock of hair is a thick unruly mop of it
the Ave Maria, the Hail Mary said on a rosary bead
a is the indefinite article
ch is the short form used for church on maps and signs

annotation.surface: A fright so great it produces a prayer and a piece written by the church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shock' offers the emotion the surface wants and means a thick mop of hair. The Ave is the Hail Mary, the three letters setters reach for whenever a prayer is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: To have a chair is to take a seat — what a host says to a visitor left standing — so the phrase amounts to an invitation to sit down.

entries.clue: Search people after one finds way to open safe (11)

indicatorNotes.after: What comes after something follows behind it, so the people are written in second even though the clue names them first.

blocks.note: to comb a field is to search every part of it
the Roman numeral for one
a nation is a people with a country of its own

annotation.surface: Frisking a crowd once somebody has worked out how to get the safe open.
annotation.walkthrough: 'After' is doing real work: it sends the people in behind the numeral rather than leaving them where the clue has them. Combing for searching is the image of going through something tooth by tooth.
annotation.definitionFit: The combination of a safe is the sequence of numbers dialled to unlock it, so it is literally the way in.

entries.clue: Charm of writer with messier style (9)

indicatorNotes.style: To style something is to arrange it the way you want it, and letters arranged afresh do not keep the order they came in.

blocks.note: the writer of the clue is the setter, who refers to themselves as me
seven letters of fodder, joined to the two above

annotation.surface: A writer whose scruffier manner is captivating.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Writer' is the setter pointing at themselves, one of the oldest conventions going, and it always gives the same two letters. 'Style' reads as manner and works as the shuffle.
annotation.definitionFit: To mesmerise someone is to hold them spellbound — the word comes from Mesmer and his hypnotism — which is charm in its older, magical sense.

entries.clue: Top gang engaged in heartless fight (5,3)

indicatorNotes.engaged in: To be engaged in something is to be busy inside it, so this chunk goes within the letters the rest of the clue supplies.
indicatorNotes.heartless: A heartless word has lost the letter at its exact centre, the one with as many letters before it as after.

blocks.note: a fight is a scrap, and the letter at its middle drops out, leaving four to open up
a crew is a gang of people working together

annotation.surface: A gang caught up in a merciless brawl.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top' is the noun, the thing you unscrew, not the adjective meaning best. 'Heartless' describes the fight in the surface and guts the word in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A screw cap is the threaded top of a bottle, the kind you twist off rather than draw a cork from.

entries.clue: Bisque soup containing blue lobster initially gets complaints (8)

indicatorNotes.soup: In a soup nothing keeps the shape it went in with, so the letters before the word go the same way.
indicatorNotes.containing: What a dish contains goes in with it, so these extra letters join the pool before it is stirred.
indicatorNotes.initially: Initially means at the outset, so only the letter each of those words starts with is used.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, the shellfish soup itself
the letters these two words start with

annotation.surface: A creamy shellfish soup with a blue lobster in it, and somebody sending it back.
annotation.walkthrough: Bisque is itself a shellfish soup, so 'bisque soup' reads as a menu and is really fodder followed by its own instruction. Two of the clue's words give up only their initials, which is how six letters fill eight squares.
annotation.definitionFit: A quibble is a petty objection, so quibbles are the small complaints raised when there is nothing larger to say.

entries.clue: Carry on in case you finally unravel seance (5,1,5)

indicatorNotes.finally: What comes finally comes last, so only the last letter of the word in front of it is used.
indicatorNotes.unravel: To unravel something is to pull it apart thread by thread, leaving the letters loose to be laid out again.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder
the letter this word finishes on
six more letters of fodder, taking the count to eleven

annotation.surface: Keep going even if the seance comes apart on you.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carry on' is the British sense of making a fuss rather than of continuing, and the surface leans hard on the wrong one. The séance loses its accent, as crossword fodder always does.
annotation.definitionFit: To carry on is to make a public fuss — 'don't carry on so' — which is what causing a scene amounts to.

entries.clue: They’re sometimes better than ‘prime numbers’, as well said? (1-5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names these by what they beat rather than offering a synonym, and the plural of the description matches the plural answer.

indicatorNotes.said: 'Said' asks for the word as it is spoken rather than as it is spelt, so what counts is the noise it makes.

blocks.note: 'as well' means besides, and besides spoken aloud comes out as a letter followed by a plural noun

annotation.surface: A claim that certain numbers beat the prime ones, agreed with out loud.
annotation.walkthrough: A single is pressed with the plugged track on one face and another on the back; 'numbers' is the music trade's word for songs, and 'prime' picks out the side the label pushed. The quotation marks flag both senses.
annotation.definitionFit: A single's B-side is the track the label did not promote, and collectors have long argued that some of them beat the hit on the front.

entries.clue: One small seabird at back of ship (6)

blocks.note: one of a thing is a thing, so a stands in for the number
s is the size on a clothing label
the tern is the fork-tailed sea bird setters reach for constantly

annotation.surface: A little gull perched at the back of a ship.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay runs straight into the definition with nothing to mark the join, which is what makes a short charade hard to see. Terns are worth banking: four letters, and every setter's sea bird.
annotation.definitionFit: Astern means at or towards the rear of a vessel — a dinghy trails astern — so it places you at the back of the ship.

entries.clue: Declines books on tablet and terminal apps (4)

indicatorNotes.on: In an across clue what is written on something has been reached after it, so the books follow the tablet rather than leading it.
indicatorNotes.terminal: A terminal letter is the one at the end of the line, so only the final letter of the word after it is taken.

blocks.note: e is the ecstasy tablet, the pill's street letter
b is short for book, and doubling a letter is how crosswords make an abbreviation plural
the letter this word ends on

annotation.surface: Book sales on tablets falling away along with the last of the apps.
annotation.walkthrough: Tablet is the pill, not the device the surface wants. 'On' is more than joinery here: across the grid it puts the books second, behind the tablet that the clue mentions after them.
annotation.definitionFit: A tide that ebbs goes out and figures that ebb fall away, so 'declines' covers the sea and the trend alike.

entries.clue: Judge lawsuits about sheep logo originally in trinket boxes (5,5)

indicatorNotes.about: To be about something is to be round it, so the letters named so far open up and take what follows inside.
indicatorNotes.originally: What a word is originally is the letter it begins with, so only that opening letter counts.

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation set before a judge's name in a law report
a lawsuit brought to court is a case
a ewe is the female sheep
the letter this word starts with

annotation.surface: A judge trying lawsuits over the brand mark on a flock.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase now more often means the hinged plastic box a CD comes in, which is where most people meet it. 'About' is the container instruction, dressed up as what a lawsuit concerns.
annotation.definitionFit: A jewel case is the small lidded box jewellery is kept in, so the plural names boxes for trinkets.

entries.clue: Rowing squad trimmed body mass (5)

indicatorNotes.trimmed: Something trimmed has had a bit taken off one end, and here it is the very first letter that comes off.

blocks.note: the mass of a body is its weight, six letters before the trimming

annotation.surface: A rowing crew that has slimmed down.
annotation.walkthrough: An eight is both the boat and the crew of rowers in it, coxed or coxless. The surface is about losing weight and the wordplay about losing a letter of it.
annotation.definitionFit: An eight is the crew of eight oarsmen who race together, and the boat they race in, so the word names the rowing squad itself.

entries.clue: Turn up high-class carpet expert (4)

indicatorNotes.Turn up: A down entry read upwards runs from its foot to its head, and anything turned up travels in that direction.

blocks.note: U is the crossword's upper-class marker, from the old 'U and non-U' split in English usage
a rug is the small carpet

annotation.surface: An upmarket rug being rolled out by somebody who knows about them.
annotation.walkthrough: The two pieces are built in clue order and only then read upwards, which is what 'turn up' asks of a down entry. U for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U vocabulary.
annotation.definitionFit: A guru is the Hindu spiritual teacher, and the word has been borrowed for anyone whose advice on a subject is treated as authority.

entries.clue: Could free student involved in government scheming (9)

indicatorNotes.free: Letters set free are no longer held in the order they were given, so they may settle anywhere.
indicatorNotes.involved: To be involved is to be drawn into the mix, so this letter joins the pool rather than standing apart from it.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
L is the learner plate on a British car, and a learner is a student
the little word joins the pool as itself, two more letters
G is the short form of government, as in the G-men who worked for it

annotation.surface: A student mixed up in some government plot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' is fodder rather than joinery, which is the hardest thing in the clue to see: it looks like the word attaching the student to the government. 'Free' reads as liberating the student and does the shuffling.
annotation.definitionFit: To collude is to plot secretly with somebody, usually against a third party, so colluding and scheming name the same underhand activity.

entries.clue: Mix up days, overwhelmed by beer (5)

indicatorNotes.overwhelmed by: To be overwhelmed by something is to be swamped underneath it, so these letters end up inside the ones that follow.

blocks.note: ale is the beer, three letters to open up
d is short for day, and doubling it makes the plural

annotation.surface: Days lost underneath too much beer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mix up' opens the clue looking exactly like an anagram instruction; it is the definition, and there are no letters to shuffle. Doubling a one-letter abbreviation to make it plural is standard — two d's for days, as pp is pages.
annotation.definitionFit: To addle somebody is to muddle their wits — an addled brain is a confused one — which is what mixing a person up does.

entries.clue: Bearing mail, regularly hurries (7)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Letters taken regularly are taken at a fixed interval, here every second one of the word that follows.

blocks.note: post is the British word for mail
every second letter of the word, counting from the second

annotation.surface: A postman rushing round with the letters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bearing' is how a person holds themselves, not a compass direction or the thing in a wheel. Alternate letters always need a decision about which letter to start on, and here it is the second.
annotation.definitionFit: Posture is the way a person carries their body — upright, slouched — which is what 'bearing' names in the sense of carriage.

entries.clue: Goes to bed at home following fainting fits? (5,2)

indicatorNotes.following: What follows something comes along behind it, so the word for being at home is written in after the other piece.

blocks.note: a funny turn is the British phrase for a dizzy spell or a faint
somebody at home is in, the way a doctor is in

annotation.surface: Heading off to bed after a run of blackouts.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a turn is one particular sort of fainting fit rather than the word's meaning. 'Following' is what sends the two-letter piece to the end instead of the front.
annotation.definitionFit: To turn in is to go to bed for the night, the phrase a host uses once the evening is over.
